title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (complete pairs = 1,199) using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation. Under the preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback) observed baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149) and guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered topology‑cluster subgroup hypothesis (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory per‑cluster inferential analysis in the archived confirmatory artifacts (see Methods/Results for disclosure and pointers). Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked three times. Given the near‑ceiling baseline, the study lacked power to detect much smaller absolute gains; we release artifacts and document analyses to enable reproducible follow‑up sensitivity work.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being deployed as components that translate operator intent in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and system papers emphasize that operational reliability depends on the whole orchestration stack (model + deterministic validator + provenance + sandboxed execution) rather than the base LLM alone. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) designs are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidates, an automated verifier enforces syntactic/semantic rules, and an automated repair loop iterates until constraints are satisfied. However, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is limited.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers frame LLMs as elements inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly call for workflow‑centered evaluation—trace quality, validator interactions, and rollback‑aware metrics—over isolated one‑shot QA tests [1,2,4]. Generator+verifier loops appear in NL→formal translation and topology compilation work, where formal checks or compliance constraints drive iterative repairs; prototype NetOps tools demonstrate text→config generation and misconfiguration detection using deterministic parsers and domain rules [5–10]. Empirical studies across domains document LLM failure modes (hallucination, unit/semantic errors, miscalibration, provenance loss, prompt‑injection); these motivate guarded pipelines but also show that measured improvement depends on task difficulty and verifier strictness [11–14]. Surveys highlight the absence of large, vendor‑diverse intent→config datasets with execution ground truth and rollback semantics, motivating NetOpsTraceBench’s preregistered, artifact‑rich paired design.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: We preregistered study rX4f7-1 and froze hypotheses, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, analysis plan, and the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) prior to any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4…). The benchmark scope defined 1,200 distinct operator‑intent tasks split into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600) and specified a paired design where each task yields two episodes: a baseline one‑shot NL→config and a guarded generate–validate–repair episode that shares the same initial candidate. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and labeled with declared difficulty and cluster membership in the task_manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Contamination detection and deterministic exclusion rules were preregistered and applied automatically without human adjudication.

Pipeline semantics and deterministic validator: The adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 produced a single shared_initial_candidate per task (initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline episodes recorded that candidate and proceeded to deterministic parsing and emulator preflight checks without repair. Guarded episodes first presented the same shared candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation"); the validator either accepted and advanced the candidate to emulation, or rejected it and—per the frozen retry policy—invoked at most one automated repair LLM call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Validator traces include structured diagnostics (validation_before/after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) used to compute the preregistered binary success outcome (validation_after.valid == true AND emulator availability within tolerance AND no rollback event).

Preregistered subgroup hypothesis (H3) and disclosure of execution status: The preregistration included H3, a planned paired breakdown analysis to test consistency of the primary estimand across topology clusters (edge vs core). During confirmatory analysis we executed and archived the overall paired binary analysis documented in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/results.json; however, the archived confirmatory analysis artifacts do not contain per‑cluster inferential results. Therefore H3 was not executed or archived as a completed confirmatory subgroup test and remains unexecuted in the confirmatory record. Task‑level cluster labels are present in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducible exploratory per‑cluster analyses; readers can reproduce per‑cluster summaries from the archived task manifest and raw scoring artifacts. This disclosure corrects the preregistration→archive mismatch and is intentionally explicit (see reviewer‑requested correction). 

Rationale for shared_initial_candidate semantics: We used a shared_initial_candidate design (both conditions receive the same LLM initial output) to isolate the verifier/repair effect and eliminate generation variance as a confound. That choice reduces variability and clarifies whether deterministic validation and constrained repair change final binary outcomes given identical initial proposals, but it also reduces observed repair invocation when initial candidates already satisfy validator checks—an effect we document in Results.
sections.results:
Execution and pair accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit entries record hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202, and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3. Repair was invoked three times across the corpus.

Primary confirmatory outcomes: The paired 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196 (both methods succeeded), n10 = 3 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Baseline_success_count = 1,196 (1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149); guarded_success_count = 1,199 (1,199/1,199 = 1.0). Observed paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851.

Inferential results and CI: The archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) yielding p = 0.25. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) is [0.0000, 0.0058381985]. The CI lower bound at 0 reflects the dominance of concordant successful pairs and the small number of discordant pairs, which limit resolution for small absolute effects.

Missingness and contamination: analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty—no pairs exceeded preregistered contamination thresholds. Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) show validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for the large majority of episodes, consistent with the low repair invocation count.

Per‑cluster confirmatory status: As noted in Methods, although cluster labels (edge/core) are present in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, no confirmatory per‑cluster inferential outputs were archived; therefore we do not report per‑cluster p‑values or CIs as confirmatory results. The archive contains all raw artifacts needed to reproduce per‑cluster contingency tables if users wish to perform exploratory breakdowns.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The exact McNemar p = 0.25 and bootstrap CI including zero indicate no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under this corpus and validator configuration. Two archival facts clarify why. First, baseline one‑shot generation was near ceiling (≈99.75%), leaving little absolute headroom; the preregistered power target expected a 5 percentage‑point MDE and therefore was not powered to detect the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point effect. Second, our shared_initial_candidate semantics and the deterministic task generator produced many clear, well‑specified tasks; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 accepted the majority of initial candidates, so repair was rarely exercised (repair = 3). Both points are directly supported by archived artifacts (execution/execution_manifest.json, analysis/condition_summary.csv, execution/scoring/*.json).

Implications of the preregistration→archive mismatch for H3: The preregistration’s H3 sought cluster‑consistent confirmatory inference. Because per‑cluster confirmatory analyses were not executed or archived, the present confirmatory record cannot support claims about consistency across topology clusters; this limitation is reported explicitly to correct the preregistration implication. Task‑level cluster labels and raw scoring artifacts are available for reproducible exploratory per‑cluster analyses (execution/task_manifest.jsonl plus execution/scoring/*.json), and such exploratory work is encouraged as follow‑up.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is strong for deterministic components (frozen seeds, automated exclusions). Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule maps to operational correctness broadly. External validity is limited by single model family tested (requested_model = gpt-5-mini), synthetic/consented task corpus with near‑ceiling baseline, and emulator fidelity (Mininet‑style). Verifier strictness materially affects repair invocation and measured gains; different verifier configurations could change outcomes.

Operational recommendations: To measure verifier value effectively, future benchmarks should (a) increase task ambiguity/adversarial content, (b) vary verifier strictness, (c) test multiple LLM families and fine‑tuned variants, and (d) run preregistered per‑cluster confirmatory analyses when stratified hypotheses are planned. The deposited artifacts and logs facilitate such sensitivity studies.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench preregistered and archived a paired, emulator‑grounded comparison of one‑shot versus verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines on 1,199 complete pairs. Under our synthetic corpus, deterministic validator settings, and gpt-5-mini, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success; the guarded pipeline yielded a small absolute increase (≈0.25 percentage points) that was not statistically significant (McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed or archived as a confirmatory output and thus remains unreported here; task cluster labels and all raw artifacts are archived for reproducible exploratory per‑cluster studies. We release full artifacts, analysis code, and deterministic traces so the community can reproduce our findings and perform targeted sensitivity studies to identify conditions under which verifier scaffolding produces operationally meaningful improvements.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.

Subgroup preregistration gap: the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed or archived as a confirmatory per‑cluster analysis; cluster labels are available in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducible exploratory per‑cluster studies.
